title: Genital Ulcer / Penile Rash in a 57-Year-Old Man
patient_instructions: You are Robert Hayes, a 57-year-old warehouse supervisor. For the past few days you have had a painful rash on your penis. You describe it as a cluster of small 'fluid-filled sacs' (blisters) on the shaft; some have started to break down. It is genuinely painful, not itchy. You have felt feverish, tired and achey, and you have noticed tender, painful lumps in your groin. This is the first time this has ever happened. You have no trouble passing urine and no penile discharge. You are embarrassed and reluctant to talk at first, but open up if the candidate is warm, reassures you about confidentiality and asks respectfully. Sexual history (only give if asked directly and sensitively): you are married but had unprotected vaginal sex with a casual female partner about a week and a half ago while away for work. You have never been diagnosed with a sexually transmitted infection. No same-sex partners, no anal or oral sex. No new soaps, creams, underwear or medications. No weight loss or loss of appetite. Your main worry, if asked: 'Is this cancer? And do I have to tell my wife?' You feel guilty and frightened. Answer questions honestly but only reveal the affair if the candidate asks about partners. Affect: anxious, softly spoken, ashamed.
candidate_instructions: You are the GP in a community general practice. Robert Hayes, a 57-year-old man, presents with a painful rash on his penis that has been present for a few days. A clinical photograph is available on request from the examiner. Your tasks: (1) Take a focused, sensitive history including a full sexual history. (2) Explain your most likely diagnosis and the key differentials to the patient. You do NOT need to perform an examination. You have 8 minutes; a prompt will be given when 6 minutes have elapsed.
examiner_instructions: Assess the candidate's ability to take a sensitive sexual-health history and reason to a diagnosis of first-episode genital herpes while retaining an appropriate safety-net. Award marks for: a confidentiality/sensitivity preamble; characterising the lesion (grouped painful vesicles, now ulcerating); associated systemic symptoms (fever, malaise, tender inguinal nodes); a complete non-judgmental sexual history (partners, gender, condom use, sites of sex, prior STIs); and screening for malignancy (weight loss, non-healing lesion). If asked, hand over the photograph showing grouped vesicular/ulcerated lesions. The candidate should name genital herpes as most likely, cite syphilis (painless indurated chancre) as the key contrast, and state that in a 57-year-old any solitary or non-healing lesion must be biopsied to exclude penile squamous cell carcinoma / erythroplasia of Queyrat. Prompt at 6 minutes: 'What is your diagnosis and what else are you considering?' Do not lead the candidate to the sexual history — it must be self-initiated.

criteria: Opens with a confidentiality and sensitivity statement; gains consent to ask personal questions
Characterises the lesion: site, onset, painful grouped vesicles/blisters, ulceration, no itch, no discharge
Elicits systemic and regional features: fever, malaise, body aches, tender inguinal lymphadenopathy, urinary symptoms
Takes a complete non-judgmental sexual history: activity, number/gender of partners, condom use, sites of sexual contact, previous STIs in patient and partners
Screens for malignancy and other causes: weight loss, appetite, non-healing/duration, new soaps/creams/underwear, new medications
States first-episode genital herpes as the most likely diagnosis with reasoning (grouped painful vesicles + fever + tender nodes)
Contrasts with syphilis (single painless indurated chancre) and lists other STI ulcers (LGV, chancroid, donovanosis)
Includes non-STI causes: fixed drug eruption, aphthous ulcers (idiopathic, NOT viral), balanitis/contact dermatitis, genital warts, shingles
Explicitly flags penile squamous cell carcinoma / erythroplasia of Queyrat as a must-not-miss in a 57-year-old
States the biopsy safety-net: any solitary or persistent/non-healing penile lesion is malignant until proven otherwise and must be biopsied
Outlines targeted investigations: HSV PCR swab of lesion base, syphilis serology (RPR/EIA) plus dark-ground/PCR, HIV and full STI screen
Outlines first-episode HSV treatment (valaciclovir 500 mg BD 5-10 days or aciclovir/famciclovir) plus analgesia and saline bathing
Addresses partner notification/contact tracing and abstinence advice for a sexually acquired ulcer
Maintains a respectful, non-judgmental, empathic manner and explains the diagnosis in plain language
Explores and addresses the patient's concerns (cancer fear, disclosure to wife) and safety-nets follow-up

red_flags: Solitary or persistent/non-healing penile ulcer in an older man - penile squamous cell carcinoma or erythroplasia of Queyrat until proven otherwise; requires biopsy
Painless indurated ulcer with regional lymphadenopathy - primary syphilitic chancre requiring dark-ground/PCR and syphilis serology and treatment
Systemic features (fever, malaise) with genital ulceration signalling first-episode disease and possible disseminated infection
Unprotected sex with a casual partner mandates HIV and full STI screening and partner notification
australian_guidelines: Therapeutic Guidelines (eTG) / ASHM - first-episode genital herpes: valaciclovir 500 mg orally BD for 5-10 days (or aciclovir 400 mg TDS, or famciclovir), with analgesia, saline bathing and counselling on recurrence and transmission

Australian STI Management Guidelines (ASHM) - genital ulcer work-up: HSV PCR from the lesion base, syphilis serology (RPR/EIA) with dark-ground microscopy/PCR, plus HIV and full STI screen; partner notification/contact tracing for any sexually acquired ulcer
RACGP / John Murtagh General Practice - any non-healing genital skin lesion warrants punch/biopsy for tissue diagnosis to exclude malignancy
Churchill's / urology principle - persistent solitary penile ulcer requires thorough investigation as malignancy is likely; always take a full sexual history
learning_objectives: Take a structured, non-judgmental sexual history that safely elicits the information needed to diagnose a genital ulcer
Differentiate painful grouped vesicular herpes from the painless indurated chancre of primary syphilis and other STI ulcers
Recognise that a persistent or solitary non-healing penile lesion in an older man requires biopsy to exclude penile squamous cell carcinoma
State the Australian investigation and treatment plan for first-episode genital herpes including partner notification
key_points: Grouped painful vesicles + fever + tender inguinal nodes in a first episode strongly favour HSV over syphilis
Aphthous ulcers are idiopathic (Behcet, IBD, trauma), NOT viral - the viral genital ulcer to name is herpes simplex
Avoid anchoring on herpes: in a 57-year-old, biopsy any solitary or non-healing lesion to exclude SCC / erythroplasia of Queyrat
A confidentiality statement and non-judgmental manner are essential to obtain an accurate sexual history and to pass the station
Contact tracing, partner notification and abstinence advice are expected scored components for any sexually acquired genital ulcer

citations.claim: Recurrence of painful genital/perineal sores is a diagnostic sign of herpes simplex, supporting first-episode genital herpes as the leading diagnosis for grouped painful vesicles.

Targeted investigation of penile lesions - VDRL for syphilitic chancre, PCR/electron microscopy for herpes, biopsy for carcinoma/erythroplasia of Queyrat - with a full sexual history; a persistent solitary ulcer needs thorough investigation as malignancy is likely.
Punch/biopsy of a skin lesion is the appropriate technique to obtain a tissue diagnosis of a non-healing genital lesion, supporting the 'any non-healing lesion -> biopsy' safety-net.
citations.source: John Murtagh General Practice, 8th Edition.pdf, p.1306
